story_text.value: I run my business on four Claude Code agents: Titus, Pheme, Davinci and Metis. They write my newsletter, The AIgent (about 9k subscribers), every day through a drafting and proofreading engine that Pheme checks before scheduling. They also build AI courses, run a pipeline that turns the day's featured repo into a talking-head video of my avatar for Instagram, set up ad deals, and run Meta ads and email funnels with me. Nothing closes until I sign off. Metis posts jobs on a job board and the others claim them. The hard part wasn't any single task. It was keeping the agents coherent over weeks. Compaction kept dropping the small decisions, and then an agent would redo work I'd already ruled out. aigent-os is my fix. At a context threshold (80% by default) the agent writes a capsule, a checkpoint file in git, and has to reply with one exact line. Only then does the runner send /clear, wait for a SessionStart receipt proving a fresh session started, and resume. One ack buys at most one clear. If anything is ambiguous it stops at HOLD:clear-stalled-after-ack and doesn't retry. On resume the capsule is reference only, live state wins, and anything the writer couldn't capture is written as Unknown. First run interviews you with three plain questions and makes a first plan. Each agent gets its own memory vault. Limits, honestly: the public evidence is 11 of 11 cycles on one Windows seat. The runner can still miss a permission dialog (#104), a seat launched from inside another Claude Code session can lose its transcript (#98), and scrolling the seat window sends stray input (#99). v1.1.0 shipped on Sunday. Try bash install.sh --dry-run, it writes nothing. I'd like to hear where the loop could still double clear or strand a session.

story_text.value:
Hi HN. Weir is for one problem: credentials crossing the boundaries of your AI agent.

For agents you build, Weir plants fake credentials where real ones would live, runs the agent's normal flows, and checks what comes out: telemetry, logs, console output, model requests, and requests to other services. It looks for those exact values, including common encoded forms, and reports where they went without printing the credential.

pip install weir-scan weir canary judge --sample

That sample shows a planted key leaking into a trace. On your own agent: pip install weir-run.

For agents you use, Weir can inventory your real credentials (it stores keyed fingerprints, never the values) and show when one enters your session or leaves in a tool call. Right now, this is supported for Claude Code. Its optional hook redacts those known credentials from tool results before the model sees them. Setup is weir statusline setup, on Linux and macOS for now.

So the two modes are deliberately different:

Build: plant → run → prove where the credential went. Use: observe → warn → optionally redact before the model sees it.

The test mode is deterministic and offline. On Linux it can also run the agent without outside network access, so direct exfiltration attempts are caught. If a required path wasn't exercised, Weir reports incomplete, never clean.

It doesn't try to detect every possible secret. It matches known whole values, so hashed, split, truncated, or otherwise transformed credentials aren't covered. The Claude Code hook only protects the tool-result boundary: it can't undo a credential already pasted into the conversation, and a failed command's output reaches the model as is.

Apache-2.0, no model in the loop, and Weir itself sends nothing anywhere. It found GHSA-j7qq-vr8c-xvw3 in MLflow (fixed in 3.17.0).

Built with AI assistance; every security finding was reproduced before I reported it.

title.value: Show HN: Weir - Catch credential leaks in the AI agents you build and use

story_text.value:
I filled email and select the reason (Account locked: My account has been locked or suspended) in https://support.github.com/contact/cannot_sign_in then submit.

A few steps to create a ticket.

After I filled everything then click submit. It show "An unexpected error occurred (status: 401)". So I never created a support ticket.

I think maybe the reason why my account was suspended:

I asked Opus 5.5 (claude code) to ask a few vendors in PRs on my own repo whether they'd offer a perk to users. It looped gh pr comment and posted the same text on 3 PRs within seconds. On the 4th call: "Your account was suspended."

Additional context: The three PRs were submitted by vendors seeking to list their MCP servers in my directory.

repo: milisp/mcp-linker

I guess Everything I login with github maybe lose if I don't use second login method.

Anyone can help?

story_text.value:
Claude Code now detects bugs in itself and offers to submit them to Anthropic. This did not cause the session to crash - so it's different than crash reports. It detected behavior that may not have been intended.

This is a product in itself...the ability to identify behavioral anomalies that might be bugs and to report them.

Pretty interesting, to say the least.

   Bug report drafted: Background Bash task reported completed (exit 0) while its process was still running                                               
  │
  │ │ - What happened: Two run_in_background Bash commands (one starting with sleep 70, one sleep 90; echo waited) each produced a "completed (exit code 0)"… │
  │ 1 to review · 2 to send · 0 to dismiss

story_text.value:
For the busy people out there, the GitHub repo has a demo video so you can see if this is worth your time: https://github.com/arcanemachine/pw-repl

The video was created by Opus 5.5; I just asked it to create a demo video (it has a 'record' tool), so I think this is a good idea of how well it can work with the tool.

---

pw-repl is a tool that makes it easy for you and your agents to work with Playwright+CDP in a browser (your current headed session, or a headless one, or both at the same time; take your pick).

It's basically a Playwright-powered swiss army knife that helps you and agents poke around your browser: Try out different features of a website, break things (e.g. mock backend responses), take screenshots, record videos, etc.

The GitHub repo shows a video, recorded by an agent using pw-repl: https://github.com/arcanemachine/pw-repl

One cool thing it can do: create videos of bug reports. You can tell an agent about a bug and to use pw-repl to capture it, and it can record a video with the built-in toast feature to narrate its actions, and show a virtual mouse to simulate actions on the screen, as if it were a user. It's also useful for capturing screenshots (which can be combined with the toast and highlight tools to emphasize certain elements or information), and has many useful features that can help agents to use it efficiently.

This isn't intended to be commercialized in any way. It's just a neat tool that I (with Claude's help) cobbled together. It's completely vibe-coded, and is intended mainly as a debugging aid. I use all the time, and hope it may be helpful for others.

It's basically just Playwright + CDP under the hood, but has some extra tools and an interface that make it easier for agents to work with.

The quickest way to try it out is to tell your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest serve --background --launch`, which starts a headless Chromium of its own. No browser setup needed. (If you don't like such `curl | bash`-esque installation instructions, read the code, or get your agent to take a look at it.)

To use it in your own browser instead, start Chrome with CDP enabled (`chrome --remote-debugging-port=9222 --user-data-dir="$HOME/.config/chrome-debug"`), and tell your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest serve --background`. (The separate `--user-data-dir` is needed because recent versions of Chrome don't open the debugging port on your default profile.)

It also can generate a skill so that you can just run `/pw-repl do some stuff`. Get your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest skill > <skills folder>/pw-repl/SKILL.md` (e.g. `~/.claude/skills/pw-repl/SKILL.md` for Claude Code).

NOTE: This has only been tested on my Linux machine, so not sure if it will work on macOS. It should, but I haven't tried it out personally.

Fun fact: This tool was originally a random REPL that Claude generated on-the-fly to do some random thing. I saw it and was blown away, so I got Claude to make it into its own application. I suspect that Claude may have taken "inspiration" from an existing project with a similar name, so credit where credit is due to this other `playwright-repl` package: https://github.com/stevez/playwright-repl

title.value: Show HN: pw-repl - A Playwright-powered REPL for you and your agents to share
